- Each of \(B,D,E\) has a color imbalance of exactly \(1\).

Thus \(B,D,E\) must each cover one more white square than black square.

The top tip \((1,5)\) can only belong to \(A,B,\) or \(C\). However, if \(B\) covers it, \(B\) must occupy

\[
(1,5),(1,4),(2,4),
\]

which contains two black squares and one white square, contradicting the coloring requirement. Neither \(D\) nor \(E\) has a legal rotation fitting around the top tip. Hence the top tip is covered by either \(A\) or \(C\).

### 2. Piece \(E\) must meet one of the left tabs

Suppose \(E\) covers none of \(U,M,L\).

- If the top is covered by \(A\), then \(B\) must cover \(U\), since neither \(C\) nor \(D\) can cover \(U\) legally. This forces \(B\) to occupy
  \[
  (2,1),(2,2),(3,2).
  \]
  The middle tab \(M\) would then have to be covered by \(C\) or \(D\), but every legal placement of either piece at \(M\) also uses \((3,2)\), causing an overlap.

- If the top is covered by \(C\), checking the only nonoverlapping ways for \(A,B,D\) to cover \(U,M,L\) leaves \(E\) with either a \(4\times2\) arrangement or a \(3\times2\) rectangle missing a bottom corner. Neither is the U-shaped piece \(E\).

Therefore \(E\) must cover at least one of \(U,M,L\).

### 3. The dot is necessarily in \(E\)

Because each left tab has only one neighboring board square, \(E\) can cover such a tab only in one of these two orientations:

\[
\begin{array}{cc}
E&E\\
 &E\\
E&E
\end{array}
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\begin{array}{cc}
E&E\\
 &E\\
E&E
\end{array}
\]

covering rows \(2\!-\!4\) or rows \(4\!-\!6\). In either case, the square \((4,2)\)—the dot—is occupied by \(E\).

For example, a complete valid filling is

\[
\begin{array}{ccccc}
\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&A&A\\
E&E&B&B&\cdot\\
\cdot&E&C&B&\cdot\\
E&E&C&C&\cdot\\
\cdot&D&D&C&\cdot\\
D&D&D&\cdot&\cdot
\end{array}
\]

and the dot is in \(E\).
